modules.title: 01. Data modeling and analytics SQL
modules.description: Design tables analysts love: OLTP versus OLAP, star schemas, grain, slowly changing dimensions and analytics SQL patterns.

lessons.title: OLTP vs OLAP, star schemas, grain and slowly changing dimensions
objectives: Explain why analytics databases are modelled differently from application databases.
Design a star schema with a clearly stated grain.
Choose SCD Type 1 or Type 2 for each dimension attribute.

topics.title: Two worlds
details: OLTP (app databases) is normalised for many small writes; OLAP (warehouses) is denormalised for big reads and aggregations.

topics.title: Star schema
details: A fact table holds measurable events at a declared grain ('one row per order line'); dimension tables describe who, what, where, when.
Surrogate keys decouple the warehouse from source system IDs.

topics.title: Slowly changing dimensions
details: Type 1 overwrites (fix a typo); Type 2 adds a new row with valid_from, valid_to and is_current to keep history (customer moved city).

reading.locator: Kimball dimensional modeling techniques: 'Four-step dimensional design process', 'Grain', 'Fact table structure', 'Dimension table structure' and 'Slowly changing dimension techniques' (types 0-2).

assignment.title: Model a retail warehouse
instructions: Pick a business process (online orders) and write the four design steps: process, grain, dimensions, facts.
Draw the star schema with fct_order_lines and dim_customer, dim_product, dim_date.
Mark each dimension attribute as SCD1 or SCD2 and explain why.
Create the tables in DuckDB/PostgreSQL with sample data.
acceptanceCriteria: The grain is stated in one sentence and every fact fits it.
SCD choices are justified.

questions.prompt: What is the grain of a fact table?
questions.answer: The level of detail one row represents.

questions.prompt: Which SCD type keeps history?
questions.answer: Type 2.
questions.explanation: It adds a new row per change with validity dates.

reviewPrompts: Explain a star schema in two sentences.

lessons.title: Analytics SQL patterns: deduplication, sessions, funnels and cohorts
objectives: Deduplicate with ROW_NUMBER and keep the latest record per key.
Build sessions from events with LAG and gaps, and funnel conversion rates.
Write cohort retention queries.

topics.title: Dedup
details: `QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) = 1` (or a subquery where QUALIFY is unsupported).

topics.title: Sessions and funnels
details: A new session starts when the gap since the previous event exceeds 30 minutes: compare with LAG and take a running SUM of the flag.
Funnels count users reaching each step in order; divide by the first step for conversion.

topics.title: Cohorts
details: Group users by signup month; for each later month count active users; present as a triangle table.

reading.locator: DuckDB docs: 'SQL introduction', 'Window functions' and the QUALIFY clause page.

assignment.title: Clickstream analytics
instructions: Generate 100,000 synthetic click events for 2,000 users with timestamps and event types.
Write SQL for: sessions, average session length, a 4-step funnel, monthly cohort retention.
Verify one result per query with a pandas implementation.
deliverables: SQL files, results and pandas checks.
acceptanceCriteria: SQL and pandas answers match.
Session logic handles the 30-minute gap correctly.

questions.prompt: How do you keep the latest row per key?
questions.answer: ROW_NUMBER over the key ordered by time descending, keep row 1.

questions.prompt: What defines a new session in this lesson?
questions.answer: A gap over 30 minutes since the user's previous event.

reviewPrompts: How do you read a cohort table?

modules.title: 02. Python for data pipelines
modules.description: Ingest data from files and APIs reliably: idempotent loads, schemas, Parquet and incremental extraction.

lessons.title: Idempotent ingestion, Parquet and incremental loads
objectives: Write ingestion that can be rerun without duplicates (idempotent).
Store data as partitioned Parquet with explicit schemas.
Load incrementally using watermarks and handle late-arriving data.

topics.title: Idempotency
details: Rerunning a job for the same date must give the same result: overwrite the partition or MERGE on keys, never blindly append.

topics.title: Parquet
details: Columnar, compressed, typed; partition by date so queries read only what they need. Avoid thousands of tiny files.

topics.title: Incremental
details: Track the last processed timestamp (watermark) and fetch only newer records with a small overlap window for late data, then deduplicate.

reading.locator: PyArrow docs: 'Reading and Writing the Apache Parquet Format' and 'Tabular Datasets' (partitioned datasets).

assignment.title: Rerunnable API loader
instructions: Ingest a paginated public API (e.g. GitHub events or a weather API) into date-partitioned Parquet.
Make reruns for the same date idempotent and add an incremental mode with a stored watermark.
Write tests: rerun gives identical files; overlap window deduplicates late records.
deliverables: Loader code, tests and a short runbook.
acceptanceCriteria: Two runs for the same date produce identical row counts and checksums.

questions.prompt: What makes a pipeline idempotent?
questions.answer: Rerunning it for the same input gives the same result with no duplicates.
questions.explanation: Overwrite partitions or MERGE on keys.

questions.prompt: Why use Parquet for analytics?
questions.answer: It is columnar, compressed and typed, so queries read less data.

modules.title: 03. Apache Spark and PySpark
modules.description: You already use PySpark in Fabric. Here you learn how Spark actually executes work so you can debug and tune it anywhere.

lessons.title: DataFrames, lazy evaluation, partitions and the Spark UI
objectives: Explain driver, executors, jobs, stages and tasks.
Explain transformations versus actions and lazy evaluation.
Read the Spark UI to find where time goes.

topics.title: Architecture
details: The driver plans work; executors run tasks on partitions in parallel. One action triggers a job made of stages separated by shuffles.

topics.title: Lazy evaluation
details: Transformations (select, filter, join) build a plan; actions (count, write) run it. `df.explain()` shows the plan the optimiser chose.

topics.title: Partitions
details: Parallelism equals the number of partitions; too few wastes cores, too many adds overhead. repartition shuffles, coalesce does not.

video.locator: Batch processing module videos on Spark internals.

reading.locator: Spark SQL, DataFrames and Datasets Guide: 'Getting Started' sections (SparkSession, creating DataFrames, untyped transformations, running SQL).

assignment.title: Local Spark investigation
instructions: Run PySpark locally (pip install pyspark) on a year of NYC taxi Parquet files.
Compute daily trip counts and average fares; inspect `explain()` and the Spark UI.
Change partition counts and record the effect on runtime and task counts.
deliverables: Notebook, Spark UI screenshots and a findings note.
acceptanceCriteria: You can point to the stage boundary caused by a shuffle.
Runtime changes are measured and explained.

questions.prompt: What triggers Spark to run work?
questions.answer: An action such as count, collect or write.

questions.prompt: What separates stages?
questions.answer: Shuffles (wide dependencies).

reviewPrompts: Explain a stage and a task.

lessons.title: Joins, shuffles, skew and performance tuning
objectives: Choose broadcast versus sort-merge joins.
Detect and fix data skew.
Use caching, partition pruning, adaptive query execution and file sizing.

topics.title: Joins
details: Broadcast a small table to every executor to avoid shuffling the big one; sort-merge for two large tables.

topics.title: Skew
details: One huge key makes one task run for ages; fix with AQE skew handling, salting or splitting the hot key.

topics.title: Tuning
details: Filter early, read only needed columns, partition output by common filters, target ~128-512 MB files, cache only reused DataFrames.

reading.locator: Spark Performance Tuning: 'Caching Data', 'Join Strategy Hints' and 'Adaptive Query Execution' (including skew join optimisation).

assignment.title: Make a slow job fast
instructions: Create a skewed join (one customer with 30% of orders) and time it.
Fix it with a broadcast hint or AQE skew handling and compare.
Write a tuning checklist from what you measured.
acceptanceCriteria: The improvement is measured on the same data and hardware.

questions.prompt: When should you broadcast a table in a join?
questions.answer: When it is small enough to fit in each executor's memory.

questions.prompt: What is data skew?
questions.answer: Uneven distribution where a few keys hold most of the data.
questions.explanation: Causes a few very slow tasks.

reviewPrompts: How do you spot skew in the UI?

modules.title: 04. Orchestration with Airflow and Dagster
modules.description: Schedule, retry, backfill and monitor pipelines. Airflow is the most requested orchestrator; Dagster's asset model is increasingly popular.

lessons.title: Airflow DAGs, scheduling, retries and backfills
objectives: Write DAGs with tasks, dependencies, schedules and retries.
Use logical dates so reruns and backfills process the right data.
Avoid common Airflow mistakes (heavy top-level code, non-idempotent tasks).

topics.title: Concepts
details: A DAG is a graph of tasks; operators define what each does; the scheduler runs them per data interval.

topics.title: Dates and backfills
details: Each run has a data interval; tasks should read only that interval so a backfill of past dates is just more runs.

topics.title: Good practice
details: Keep DAG files light (no heavy imports or queries at parse time); make tasks idempotent; pass small metadata, not data, between tasks.

reading.locator: Airflow 'Core Concepts': DAGs, DAG Runs, Tasks, Operators and the scheduler pages; then the tutorial 'Fundamental Concepts'.

assignment.title: Daily pipeline with backfill
instructions: Run Airflow locally with Docker Compose.
Write a DAG that ingests one day of your API data, loads it to DuckDB/PostgreSQL and runs a quality check.
Backfill the last 14 days and prove reruns do not duplicate data.
deliverables: DAG code, compose file and backfill evidence.
acceptanceCriteria: Backfilled and rerun days have correct, non-duplicated counts.

questions.prompt: What should a task read when backfilling?
questions.answer: Only its run's data interval.

questions.prompt: Why keep top-level DAG code light?
questions.answer: The scheduler parses DAG files often.
questions.explanation: Heavy code slows the whole system.

reviewPrompts: What makes a task safe to retry?

lessons.title: Dagster assets, partitions and sensors
objectives: Model pipelines as software-defined assets.
Use daily partitions and backfills in Dagster.
Trigger runs from sensors and attach checks to assets.

topics.title: Assets
details: You declare the tables/files that should exist and how to build each from upstream assets; Dagster derives the graph.

topics.title: Partitions
details: Daily partitions map to date ranges; materialise one partition or backfill many.

topics.title: Checks
details: Asset checks run after materialisation (row counts, freshness) and show status in the UI.

reading.locator: Dagster docs: 'Getting started', then concepts pages for assets, partitions, schedules/sensors and asset checks.

assignment.title: Rebuild the pipeline as assets
instructions: Rebuild your Airflow pipeline in Dagster as assets with daily partitions.
Add two asset checks and a sensor for a new file arriving.
Write a comparison of Airflow and Dagster from your experience.
acceptanceCriteria: Partitions backfill correctly and checks run.

questions.prompt: What is a software-defined asset?
questions.answer: A declared data artifact plus the code that builds it from upstream assets.

questions.prompt: What does an asset check do?
questions.answer: Validates an asset after it is built.
questions.explanation: For example row counts or freshness.

reviewPrompts: When would you use a sensor?

modules.title: 05. Analytics engineering with dbt
modules.description: Transform data with SQL using software practices: modular models, tests, documentation, incremental builds and snapshots.

lessons.title: dbt models, sources, tests and documentation
objectives: Structure a dbt project into sources, staging, intermediate and marts.
Use ref() and source() so dbt builds the dependency graph.
Add generic and custom tests and generate documentation.

topics.title: Project layout
details: staging: one model per source table, light cleaning; intermediate: joins and logic; marts: facts and dimensions for users.

topics.title: ref and source
details: `{{ ref('stg_orders') }}` links models; dbt builds them in order and draws lineage.

topics.title: Tests and docs
details: unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships; custom SQL tests for business rules; `dbt docs generate` publishes a searchable catalog.

video.locator: dbt sections of the analytics engineering module.

reading.locator: dbt docs: 'About dbt models', then 'Add data tests to your DAG' and the 'sources' and 'documentation' pages linked from it.

assignment.title: dbt on DuckDB
instructions: Set up dbt-duckdb on NYC taxi data (one or two months to start).
Build staging, intermediate and mart models for a trips star schema.
Add 20+ tests including a custom one for impossible trips; generate docs.
acceptanceCriteria: `dbt build` passes; a planted bad row makes a test fail.

questions.prompt: What does ref() give you?
questions.answer: Dependency ordering and lineage between models.

questions.prompt: Name four generic dbt tests.
questions.answer: unique, not_null, accepted_values, relationships.

reviewPrompts: How do dbt tests fail a build?

lessons.title: Incremental models, snapshots and CI for dbt
objectives: Build incremental models that process only new data.
Maintain SCD Type 2 history with snapshots.
Run dbt in CI on changed models only.

topics.title: Incremental
details: `materialized='incremental'` with `is_incremental()` filters to new rows; choose a merge strategy and unique_key; full refresh when logic changes.

topics.title: Snapshots
details: Snapshots compare source rows over time and keep history with dbt_valid_from/dbt_valid_to.

topics.title: CI
details: `dbt build --select state:modified+` builds only changed models and their children in CI.

reading.locator: dbt docs: 'Incremental models' (configuring, is_incremental, unique_key, strategies) and then 'Snapshots'.

assignment.title: Scale to a billion rows
instructions: Convert fct_trips to incremental by month; load many months of NYC taxi data.
Compare full-refresh and incremental build times.
Add a snapshot for a zone dimension and a GitHub Actions CI job running changed models.
deliverables: Timings table, snapshot output and CI workflow.
acceptanceCriteria: Incremental runs process only new months.
CI runs on pull requests.

questions.prompt: What does is_incremental() let you do?
questions.answer: Filter to only new rows on incremental runs.

questions.prompt: Which dbt feature keeps SCD2 history?
questions.answer: Snapshots.

reviewPrompts: When do you need a full refresh?

modules.title: 06. Streaming with Kafka and Spark Structured Streaming
modules.description: Process events continuously: Kafka fundamentals, stream processing with watermarks and state, and exactly-once results.

lessons.title: Kafka fundamentals: topics, partitions, producers and consumer groups
objectives: Explain topics, partitions, offsets, replication and retention.
Write a producer with keys and a consumer group in Python.
Explain ordering guarantees and delivery semantics.

topics.title: Model
details: A topic is an append-only log split into partitions; each message has an offset. Messages with the same key go to the same partition, keeping their order.

topics.title: Consumers
details: A consumer group shares partitions among members; each partition is read by one member. Committed offsets record progress.

topics.title: Semantics
details: At-most-once (commit before processing), at-least-once (commit after) and exactly-once (transactions or idempotent sinks).

reading.locator: Kafka 'Introduction' page in full, then the documentation sections on producer acks and consumer groups.

assignment.title: Click events into Kafka
instructions: Run Kafka in Docker (KRaft mode).
Write a Python producer sending keyed click events and a consumer group of three consumers.
Kill a consumer mid-stream and show rebalancing; show per-key ordering is preserved.
acceptanceCriteria: Rebalancing is shown and no messages are lost with at-least-once commits.

questions.prompt: How does Kafka keep order for one customer's events?
questions.answer: By using the customer ID as the message key, so they go to the same partition.

questions.prompt: What is a consumer group?
questions.answer: Consumers that share a topic's partitions, each partition read by one member.

reviewPrompts: What decides the number of parallel consumers?

lessons.title: Structured Streaming: triggers, watermarks, state and checkpoints
objectives: Write a streaming query from Kafka to a table with checkpoints.
Use event-time windows and watermarks for late data.
Deduplicate streams and recover after a restart.

topics.title: Streaming as tables
details: Structured Streaming treats a stream as an unbounded table processed in micro-batches; the checkpoint stores offsets and state.

topics.title: Event time
details: Window by when the event happened, not when it arrived. A watermark (e.g. 10 minutes) says how late data may be before state is dropped.

topics.title: Recovery
details: Restarting with the same checkpoint resumes exactly where it left off; idempotent or transactional sinks prevent duplicates.

reading.locator: Structured Streaming guide: 'Quick Example', 'Programming Model', 'Window Operations on Event Time', 'Handling Late Data and Watermarking' and 'Recovering from Failures with Checkpointing'.

assignment.title: Windowed counts with late data
instructions: Read your Kafka click topic with Spark, compute 5-minute event-time counts with a 10-minute watermark, write to Parquet/Delta.
Send late and duplicate events and show how they are handled.
Kill and restart the job; prove results have no duplicates.
deliverables: Streaming job, test event script and results.
acceptanceCriteria: Late events within the watermark are counted; later ones are dropped and explained.
Restart produces no duplicates.

questions.prompt: What does a watermark control?
questions.answer: How long to wait for late events before finalising and dropping state.

questions.prompt: What is stored in a streaming checkpoint?
questions.answer: Source offsets and operator state.

reviewPrompts: How do you avoid duplicates on restart?

modules.title: 07. Lakehouse table formats: Delta Lake and Iceberg
modules.description: Open table formats add transactions, schema evolution and time travel to files in object storage. Fabric uses Delta; Iceberg is widely adopted across clouds.

lessons.title: Delta Lake: transactions, MERGE, schema evolution and time travel
objectives: Explain the transaction log and how it gives ACID on files.
Upsert with MERGE and evolve schemas safely.
Use time travel, OPTIMIZE/Z-ordering and VACUUM.

topics.title: Log
details: Every commit writes a JSON entry listing added/removed files; readers see a consistent snapshot.

topics.title: Operations
details: MERGE INTO target USING updates ON key WHEN MATCHED UPDATE WHEN NOT MATCHED INSERT: the basis of upserts and SCD2.
Schema evolution adds columns with mergeSchema; dropping or retyping needs care.

topics.title: Maintenance
details: Compact small files (OPTIMIZE), cluster for filters (Z-order/liquid clustering), and VACUUM old files after the retention period.

reading.locator: Delta Lake docs: 'Quickstart', then 'Table deletes, updates, and merges', 'Table batch reads and writes' (time travel) and the schema evolution sections.

assignment.title: Delta table lifecycle
instructions: Create a Delta table locally with delta-spark; upsert three batches with MERGE.
Add a column via schema evolution; time-travel to version 1 and compare.
Write many small files, OPTIMIZE them, and measure query time before and after.
acceptanceCriteria: MERGE results match an expected table.
Compaction effect is measured.

questions.prompt: How does Delta give ACID on files?
questions.answer: Through a transaction log recording each commit's file changes.

questions.prompt: What does VACUUM remove?
questions.answer: Data files no longer referenced by recent table versions.

reviewPrompts: Write a MERGE statement for upserts.

lessons.title: Apache Iceberg: catalogs, hidden partitioning and maintenance
objectives: Explain Iceberg metadata (snapshots, manifests) and catalogs.
Use hidden partitioning and partition evolution.
Run maintenance: compaction, snapshot expiry and orphan file removal.

topics.title: Metadata
details: A catalog points to the current metadata file; snapshots list manifests, which list data files with column stats used to skip files.

topics.title: Partitioning
details: Hidden partitioning (e.g. days(event_ts)) means queries filter on the column and Iceberg prunes automatically; the partition spec can evolve.

topics.title: Maintenance
details: rewrite_data_files compacts; expire_snapshots and remove_orphan_files control storage; schedule them in your orchestrator.

reading.locator: Iceberg docs: 'Introduction', the Spark quickstart, 'Partitioning' (hidden partitioning) and 'Maintenance'.

assignment.title: Iceberg on MinIO
instructions: Run Spark + Iceberg (REST or JDBC catalog) + MinIO in Docker Compose.
Create a table partitioned by days(event_ts), write data, then evolve to hours().
Query with Trino and run compaction and snapshot expiry; record file counts before and after.
deliverables: Compose stack, scripts and before/after metrics.
acceptanceCriteria: Partition evolution works without rewriting old data.
Maintenance reduces file count.

questions.prompt: What is hidden partitioning?
questions.answer: Iceberg derives partitions from column transforms so queries need not reference partition columns.

questions.prompt: What do manifests store?
questions.answer: Lists of data files with column statistics.

reviewPrompts: Which maintenance jobs would you schedule?

modules.title: 08. Change data capture
modules.description: Stream every insert, update and delete from operational databases into the lake, and maintain history with SCD Type 2.

lessons.title: Debezium CDC into SCD Type 2 tables
objectives: Explain log-based CDC versus query-based extraction.
Configure Debezium for PostgreSQL with Kafka Connect.
Apply change events in order into an SCD2 table with MERGE.

topics.title: Why log-based
details: Reading the database's write-ahead log captures deletes and every change with low load; polling misses deletes and intermediate states.

topics.title: Debezium events
details: Each event has before/after images, op (c, u, d, r) and source position; snapshots ('r') load existing rows first.

topics.title: Applying changes
details: Order events per key by source position, then close the current SCD2 row (set valid_to) and insert the new one; deletes close without inserting.
Replaying the same events must give the same table.

video.locator: Whole video (concepts transfer beyond Azure SQL).

reading.locator: Debezium PostgreSQL connector docs: 'Overview', 'How the connector works' (snapshots, streaming changes) and 'Data change events'.

assignment.title: CDC pipeline
instructions: Run PostgreSQL (wal_level=logical), Kafka, Kafka Connect with Debezium in Docker Compose.
Generate inserts, updates, deletes and a schema change on a customers table.
Write a PySpark job that MERGEs events into a Delta SCD2 table; verify against a hand-computed expected table.
Replay all events and show the result is identical.
deliverables: Compose stack, connector config, job and verification.
acceptanceCriteria: The SCD2 table matches the expected history exactly.
Replay is idempotent.

questions.prompt: Why is log-based CDC better than polling?
questions.answer: It captures deletes and every change with low source load.

questions.prompt: How does a delete affect an SCD2 table?
questions.answer: The current row is closed (valid_to set) without a new row.

reviewPrompts: How do you guarantee ordering per key?

modules.title: 09. Data quality and contracts
modules.description: Catch bad data before users do: expectations, quarantines, contracts between producers and consumers, and reconciliation.

lessons.title: Great Expectations, quarantine tables and data contracts
objectives: Write expectation suites for completeness, validity, uniqueness and freshness.
Route failing records to quarantine without stopping good data.
Define data contracts and reconcile source and target counts.

topics.title: Dimensions of quality
details: Completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness; pick checks per column and per table.

topics.title: Handling failures
details: Block the pipeline for critical failures; quarantine bad rows with the failure reason for others; alert owners.

topics.title: Contracts
details: A contract fixes schema, types and semantics a producer promises; breaking changes require versioning and notice. dbt model contracts enforce shape at build time.

reading.locator: Great Expectations docs: overview, then 'Create Expectations', 'Run validations' (checkpoints) and 'Data Docs'.

assignment.title: Quality gate
instructions: Write a 40-expectation suite for your CDC or taxi data.
Add a quarantine path and a daily reconciliation report (source vs target counts and sums).
Plant five kinds of bad data and show each is caught.
acceptanceCriteria: All planted issues are caught and routed correctly.

questions.prompt: Why quarantine instead of failing the whole pipeline?
questions.answer: Good data keeps flowing while bad rows are isolated for review.

questions.prompt: What is a data contract?
questions.answer: An agreed schema and meaning a producer guarantees to consumers.

reviewPrompts: What goes in a reconciliation report?

modules.title: 10. Warehouses, query engines and cost
modules.description: Choose and tune analytical engines: DuckDB for local work, Snowflake as a cloud warehouse, Trino for federation, and measure cost.

lessons.title: DuckDB, Snowflake and Trino: when to use which
objectives: Explain columnar engines, separation of storage and compute, and federation.
Run the same model on DuckDB and (optionally) a Snowflake trial.
Query lake tables and a database together with Trino.

topics.title: Engines
details: DuckDB: in-process, great for local analytics up to large single-machine data. Snowflake: managed warehouse with elastic virtual warehouses. Trino: distributed SQL over many sources.

topics.title: Storage and compute
details: Separating them lets you scale compute up for a job and down after; you pay for compute time and storage separately.

topics.title: Federation
details: Trino joins Iceberg tables with PostgreSQL in one query; push filters down to sources to keep it fast.

reading.locator: Snowflake docs: 'Overview of warehouses' and 'Warehouse considerations'; then 'Micro-partitions & Data Clustering'.

assignment.title: Same model, three engines
instructions: Run your dbt marts on DuckDB; optionally load a sample into a Snowflake trial and run there (delete afterwards).
Use Trino to join your Iceberg clicks with a PostgreSQL users table.
Write a decision guide: which engine for which workload and why.
acceptanceCriteria: Timings list data size and hardware/warehouse size.
Trial resources are deleted.

questions.prompt: Benefit of separating storage and compute?
questions.answer: Scale and pay for compute independently of stored data.
questions.explanation: Run big jobs on big warehouses briefly.

questions.prompt: What is query federation?
questions.answer: Querying several data sources in one SQL statement.

lessons.title: Performance and cost tuning for analytical workloads
objectives: Find expensive queries and explain why they are expensive.
Apply partitioning, clustering, incremental builds and pre-aggregation.
Estimate and report cost per pipeline run.

topics.title: Measure first
details: Use query history/profiles to find the top cost queries; look at bytes scanned and spilled.

topics.title: Fixes
details: Prune with partitions/clustering, avoid SELECT *, materialise expensive joins, incremental builds, right-size compute and auto-suspend.

topics.title: FinOps
details: Tag resources by pipeline, report cost per run, set budgets and alerts.

reading.locator: FinOps Framework overview: principles, phases (inform, optimize, operate) and the capabilities list.

assignment.title: Halve a pipeline's cost
instructions: Pick your most expensive dbt model; record bytes scanned and runtime.
Apply two optimisations and re-measure.
Write a one-page cost report with before/after numbers.
acceptanceCriteria: Numbers come from recorded runs on the same data.

questions.prompt: Main driver of warehouse query cost?
questions.answer: Data scanned and compute time.

questions.prompt: Why avoid SELECT * in analytics?
questions.answer: Columnar engines then read every column.

reviewPrompts: How do you report cost per pipeline?

modules.title: 11. Lineage, governance and privacy
modules.description: Know where every number comes from and who may see it: lineage, catalogs, PII handling and access control.

lessons.title: Lineage with OpenLineage, data catalogs and PII protection
objectives: Emit and view lineage for jobs and datasets.
Classify sensitive columns and apply masking and access controls.
Use lineage for impact analysis before changing a model.

topics.title: Lineage
details: OpenLineage events describe runs, jobs and input/output datasets (and column-level lineage when available); tools like Marquez visualise them.

topics.title: Governance
details: A catalog lists datasets, owners, descriptions and quality; access follows least privilege; audit who read what.

topics.title: Privacy
details: Identify PII, minimise it, mask or tokenise it in analytics, and honour deletion requests across copies.

reading.locator: OpenLineage docs: 'About OpenLineage', 'Object model' and the integration page for dbt or Airflow.

assignment.title: Lineage and impact analysis
instructions: Emit OpenLineage events from your dbt or Airflow pipeline into a local Marquez.
Tag PII columns and create a masked view for analysts.
Use the lineage graph to list everything affected if a source column is renamed.
deliverables: Screenshots, masked view and impact analysis.
acceptanceCriteria: The impact list matches the lineage graph.
Analysts cannot see unmasked PII.

questions.prompt: What is lineage used for?
questions.answer: Tracing data origins and finding downstream impact of changes.

questions.prompt: Name one way to protect PII in analytics.
questions.answer: Masking or tokenising the columns.

reviewPrompts: What does an OpenLineage event contain?
How do you handle a deletion request?

limitations: Skill-builder lessons are beginner-first: each one assumes you have not used the tool before and explains the vocabulary before the practice.
Readings are official documentation or free books, linked rather than copied. Check the current version when you open a link; tools change.
Use your own machine, free tiers and synthetic or public data. Never use employer code, client data or credentials in exercises.
You already build Fabric/PySpark pipelines at work. These lessons use open-source tools locally so your portfolio does not depend on employer systems or paid capacity.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Model data dimensionally and write analytics SQL and idempotent Python ingestion.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A star schema with documented grain and an ingestion script that can be rerun safely.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Process data with Spark, orchestrate with Airflow/Dagster and transform with tested dbt models.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A scheduled batch pipeline with tests and backfills.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Build streaming pipelines with Kafka and Spark Structured Streaming on Delta/Iceberg tables, including CDC.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A streaming lakehouse that survives restarts without duplicates, plus SCD2 from CDC.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Guarantee data quality, tune warehouse cost/performance and govern data with lineage.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Quality suites in CI, measured performance improvements and lineage graphs.
